title: Seizure

rationale.Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych: AMS, hallucinations, tremors, hyperreflexia. Seizure activity.
rationale.CIWA-Ar scoring: Quantifies withdrawal severity. Guides benzodiazepine dosing. Score >15 = severe withdrawal.
rationale.CBC: Screening. Anemia, thrombocytopenia common in AUD.
rationale.BMP / CMP: Electrolyte abnormalities — hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia. Check Mg, Phos, K.
rationale.Toxicology screen (urine/serum): Confirm co-ingestants. Rule out other toxidromes.
rationale.CT head without contrast: New-onset seizure — rule out intracranial hemorrhage, trauma, mass.
rationale.EEG: If seizure vs DT tremor unclear. Rule out non-convulsive status epilepticus.
rationale.Thiamine (IV/IM): Thiamine BEFORE glucose to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
rationale.Benzodiazepine (Diazepam / Lorazepam / C: First-line for alcohol withdrawal. Symptom-triggered per CIWA or fixed-schedule. Titrate to sedation but arousable.
rationale.IV fluids (NS / LR with electrolytes): Dehydration from diaphoresis, poor intake. Correct electrolytes.
rationale.Magnesium / Potassium replacement: Hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia common in AUD — correct.
rationale.Admit to ICU: Delirium tremens requires ICU for continuous CIWA monitoring, IV benzodiazepines, and management of autonomic instability.
rationale.Glucose without thiamine first: Giving glucose before thiamine in alcoholic/malnourished patients can PRECIPITATE Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Always give thiamine first.
rationale.Antipsychotics (haloperidol) as monother: Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold — dangerous in alcohol withdrawal. Benzodiazepines are first-line. Antipsychotics only as adjunct for severe hallucination/agitation.

hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with new-onset seizure, altered mental status, autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, hyperthermia), tremors, and visual/tactile hallucinations (formication). History reveals chronic heavy alcohol use with abrupt cessation 24-72 hours prior. This is alcohol withdrawal progressing to delirium tremens — a medical emergency with 5-15% mortality if untreated. Pathophysiology: chronic alcohol enhances GABA inhibition and suppresses NMDA glutamate excitation. Abrupt withdrawal → loss of GABA tone + rebound glutamate hyperactivity → CNS hyperexcitability. The CIWA-Ar score quantifies severity and guides treatment. Management: benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) — symptom-triggered or fixed-schedule dosing until sedated but arousable. Thiamine before glucose (prevent Wernicke's). IV fluids for dehydration. Correct electrolytes (hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia common). Admit to ICU for severe DTs. Rule out other causes of seizure: CT head, EEG, tox screen, metabolic panel.
